title: Case Study: Parking Lot
summary: Design a multi-level parking lot end to end — entities, classes, patterns, and the concurrency bug everyone misses.

blocks.markdown:
**Design a parking lot**: a multi-level facility that assigns spots to different vehicle types, tracks time with a ticket, charges on exit, and never double-books a spot even when two cars arrive at once.

- It's a favorite LLD interview because it forces **entity modeling**, **pattern selection**, and a real **concurrency** decision in one problem.
- The full solution uses Singleton, Factory, and Strategy together — see [creational-patterns](creational-patterns) and [behavioral-patterns-i](behavioral-patterns-i).
- Use [lld-interview-framework](lld-interview-framework) as the general approach; this topic is that framework applied end to end.

blocks.subTitle: Functional
blocks.markdown:
What the system must do:

- **Multiple levels (floors)**, each with a fixed number of spots.
- **Spot types**: compact, large, handicapped, motorcycle — a vehicle can only park in a spot sized for it.
- **Park / unpark** a vehicle, picking the nearest available matching spot.
- **Ticketing**: issue a ticket on entry with a timestamp; use it to compute the fee on exit.
- **Pricing**: fee depends on duration and vehicle type.
- **Multiple entry and exit gates** operating at the same time.

blocks.subTitle: Non-functional
blocks.markdown:
What the system must guarantee, not just do:

- **Concurrency safety** — with multiple gates, two attendants must never hand out the same spot to two cars.
- **Consistency** — spot availability must reflect reality at all times, not a stale cache.
- **Extensibility** — new spot types, pricing schemes, or payment methods should slot in without rewriting the core.

Non-functional requirements shape the *design*, not just the feature list — concurrency alone decides how `ParkingSpot` allocation is written.

**Noun extraction**: underline the nouns in the requirements and each becomes a candidate class.

| Noun in requirements | Becomes |
|---|---|
| parking lot, floor, spot | `ParkingLot`, `ParkingFloor`, `ParkingSpot` |
| car, bike, truck | `Vehicle` hierarchy |
| ticket, gate | `Ticket`, `EntryGate` / `ExitGate` |

Verbs matter too: "picks a spot" and "computes a fee" are behaviors that don't belong on a data class — they become **strategies** (`ParkingStrategy`, `PricingStrategy`).

blocks.subTitle: ParkingLot — Singleton
blocks.markdown:
The lot is the single coordinating object — exactly one exists per physical facility, so it's a **Singleton**.

```text
class ParkingLot:
    private static instance = null
    private floors: List<ParkingFloor>
    private parkingStrategy: ParkingStrategy
    private pricingStrategy: PricingStrategy

    private constructor(floors, parkingStrategy, pricingStrategy):
        this.floors = floors
        this.parkingStrategy = parkingStrategy
        this.pricingStrategy = pricingStrategy

    static method getInstance(): ParkingLot:
        if instance == null:
            instance = new ParkingLot(loadFloors(), new NearestSpotStrategy(), new HourlyPricingStrategy())
        return instance

    method parkVehicle(vehicle: Vehicle): Ticket:
        spot = parkingStrategy.findSpot(floors, vehicle.type)
        if spot == null:
            throw LotFullException()
        spot.assign(vehicle)          // atomic claim, see Concurrency card
        return new Ticket(vehicle, spot, now())

    method unparkVehicle(ticket: Ticket): Money:
        ticket.exitTime = now()
        fee = pricingStrategy.calculateFee(ticket)
        ticket.spot.release()
        return fee
```

blocks.subTitle: ParkingFloor & ParkingSpot
blocks.markdown:
A floor is a container of spots; a spot knows its own type and status.

```text
enum SpotType:
    COMPACT
    LARGE
    HANDICAPPED
    MOTORCYCLE

class ParkingSpot:
    id: String
    type: SpotType
    isFree: boolean = true
    private lock: Mutex

    method assign(vehicle: Vehicle):
        lock.acquire()
        try:
            if not isFree:
                throw SpotTakenException()
            isFree = false
        finally:
            lock.release()

    method release():
        isFree = true

class ParkingFloor:
    level: int
    spots: List<ParkingSpot>

    method availableSpots(type: SpotType): List<ParkingSpot>:
        return spots.filter(s -> s.isFree and s.type == type)
```

blocks.subTitle: Vehicle hierarchy
blocks.markdown:
Each vehicle knows which spot type it needs — that mapping lives on the vehicle, not scattered in `if` chains elsewhere.

```text
abstract class Vehicle:
    licensePlate: String
    abstract requiredSpotType(): SpotType

class Car extends Vehicle:
    method requiredSpotType(): SpotType:
        return SpotType.COMPACT

class Bike extends Vehicle:
    method requiredSpotType(): SpotType:
        return SpotType.MOTORCYCLE

class Truck extends Vehicle:
    method requiredSpotType(): SpotType:
        return SpotType.LARGE

// creation goes through a factory, not scattered "new Car()" calls
class VehicleFactory:
    static method create(kind: String, plate: String): Vehicle:
        switch kind:
            case "car": return new Car(plate)
            case "bike": return new Bike(plate)
            case "truck": return new Truck(plate)
```

blocks.subTitle: Ticket
blocks.markdown:
The ticket is the receipt that links a vehicle to a spot for the duration of its stay — it's the object both gates read and write.

```text
class Ticket:
    id: String
    vehicle: Vehicle
    spot: ParkingSpot
    entryTime: DateTime
    exitTime: DateTime = null

    constructor(vehicle, spot, entryTime):
        this.id = generateId()
        this.vehicle = vehicle
        this.spot = spot
        this.entryTime = entryTime

    method durationInHours(): float:
        return hoursBetween(entryTime, exitTime ?? now())
```

blocks.subTitle: EntryGate & ExitGate
blocks.markdown:
Gates are thin — they only translate a physical event into a call on the lot. Multiple gates can call the same `ParkingLot` singleton concurrently.

```text
class EntryGate:
    id: String
    lot: ParkingLot

    method handleArrival(vehicleKind, plate): Ticket:
        vehicle = VehicleFactory.create(vehicleKind, plate)
        return lot.parkVehicle(vehicle)   // may race with other gates

class ExitGate:
    id: String
    lot: ParkingLot

    method handleDeparture(ticket: Ticket): Money:
        fee = lot.unparkVehicle(ticket)
        printReceipt(ticket, fee)
        return fee
```

blocks.subTitle: ParkingStrategy — finding a spot
PricingStrategy — computing the fee
blocks.markdown:
Pricing rules change often (holiday rates, vehicle-based rates) — keeping it as a strategy avoids editing `ParkingLot` every time finance changes a number.

```text
interface PricingStrategy:
    method calculateFee(ticket: Ticket): Money

class HourlyPricingStrategy implements PricingStrategy:
    private rates = { COMPACT: 20, LARGE: 40, HANDICAPPED: 10, MOTORCYCLE: 10 }

    method calculateFee(ticket): Money:
        hours = ceil(ticket.durationInHours())
        rate = rates[ticket.spot.type]
        return Money(hours * rate)
```

Where each pattern earns its place in this design:

| Pattern | Where it's used |
|---|---|
| Singleton | `ParkingLot` — one facility, one coordinator |
| Factory | `VehicleFactory` builds Car/Bike/Truck from a type string |
| Strategy | `ParkingStrategy` (spot allocation) and `PricingStrategy` (fee) |

None of these are decorative — each replaces an `if/else` chain that would otherwise live inside `ParkingLot`. See [creational-patterns](creational-patterns) and [behavioral-patterns-i](behavioral-patterns-i) for the general form of each.

blocks.subTitle: Two cars, one spot
blocks.markdown:
**The classic bug**: two cars pull up to different entry gates at the same instant, both see the same last free spot as available, and both get a ticket for it.

- The race happens because "check if free" and "mark as taken" are two separate steps — a **check-then-act** race condition.
- Fix: make the claim **atomic** inside `ParkingSpot.assign()` with a lock — one gate acquires the lock, sees it's free, marks it taken, and releases; the second gate then sees it's already taken and moves on.
- At scale, a per-spot mutex is replaced by a **compare-and-swap** on the spot's status, or the whole allocation is pushed into a database transaction so it survives across servers.

How the design absorbs real follow-up requirements without a rewrite:

- **EV charging spots** — add `SpotType.ELECTRIC` and an `EvChargingSpot` subclass with a `chargingRate` field; `ParkingStrategy` and `VehicleFactory` need no changes.
- **Monthly passes** — add a `PassPricingStrategy` that returns zero fee for pass holders; swapped in at the `ParkingLot` construction site, nothing else moves.
- **Trade-off**: the strategy interfaces add a layer of indirection that's overkill for a lot with one fixed price — good design fits the scale of change you actually expect, not every hypothetical.

blocks.subTitle: Modeling spot types
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you model different parking spot types?**

An enum (`SpotType`: COMPACT, LARGE, HANDICAPPED, MOTORCYCLE) on `ParkingSpot`, plus a `requiredSpotType()` method on `Vehicle` so each vehicle declares what it needs. Avoid a `ParkingSpot` subclass per type unless spots genuinely behave differently (e.g. an EV spot that also tracks charging) — otherwise an enum is simpler and just as correct.

blocks.subTitle: Which patterns fit
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Which design patterns fit a parking lot, and why?**

Singleton for `ParkingLot` — one facility must have one source of truth for spot state. Factory for building `Vehicle` instances from an entry-gate input without the gate knowing concrete classes. Strategy for both spot allocation and pricing, since both rules change independently of the core lot logic and of each other.

blocks.subTitle: Finding the nearest free spot
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you find the nearest free spot efficiently?**

Don't scan every spot on every request. Keep a per-floor, per-type count (or an index/free-list) of available spots so you can skip full floors immediately, and only scan the spot list within a floor that already reports availability. This is exactly the `ParkingStrategy` abstraction — the naive linear scan in the pseudocode is correct but would be swapped for an indexed version under real load.

blocks.subTitle: Two cars racing for one spot
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you handle two cars racing for the last free spot?**

Make the read-and-claim a single atomic operation instead of a separate check then update. In-process, a lock inside `ParkingSpot.assign()` is enough. Across multiple servers, use a database-level atomic update (`UPDATE spots SET is_free = false WHERE id = ? AND is_free = true`) and check the affected row count — zero rows means someone else won the race, so retry with the next candidate spot.

blocks.subTitle: Extending for EV charging
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How would you extend this design for EV charging spots?**

Add `SpotType.ELECTRIC` and let `ParkingSpot` (or a subclass) carry a `chargingRate` and `isCharging` flag. `VehicleFactory` gains an `ElectricCar` whose `requiredSpotType()` returns `ELECTRIC`. `PricingStrategy` gets a variant that adds a per-kWh charge. No change is needed to `ParkingLot`, `ParkingFloor`, or the gates — that's the payoff of pushing variation into enums and strategies instead of hardcoding it.

blocks.subTitle: Why not one giant ParkingLot class
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why not just put all the logic in one big `ParkingLot` class?**

It would work at first, but every new pricing rule or allocation policy would mean editing and re-testing that one class — violating the **open/closed principle**. Splitting allocation into `ParkingStrategy` and pricing into `PricingStrategy` means `ParkingLot` stays stable while those policies evolve, and each can be unit-tested in isolation from the rest of the system.

blocks.subTitle: Multiple entry and exit gates
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How do multiple entry and exit gates stay consistent with each other?**

They all operate on the same `ParkingLot` singleton and the same underlying spot state — a gate never keeps its own copy of availability. Combined with the per-spot lock (or atomic DB update) from the concurrency card, every gate always reads and writes the one shared source of truth, so no gate can act on stale data.
